I: The Habsburg Miracles The Battle of Vienna (1683) ​ On September 8, 1683, the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived in Vienna. On this holy day, priests, citizens, and soldiers alike poured into the churches of Vienna or failing that, their steps, and prayed. For unlike any previous nativity, this one had been one that many expected to live to see. For two months, Vienna had been surrounded by more than 150,000 Turkish soldiers commanded by the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa, Pasha, himself. This mighty host had cut off Vienna entirely from the rest of the Christian world and bombarded it daily while the Ottoman trenches steadily advanced upon the city. The Austrian army and band of citizens that had been left behind by their frightened Emperor Leopold numbered less than 20,000. Their situation was desperate and even their stalwart garrison commander, Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg, could sense that the city would not survive much longer, and once the Ottomans broke through its walls everyone knew that only a bloody execution awaited every one of them. In the grips of this terrible situation, Starhemberg and the defenders of Vienna could do nothing more than pray for deliverance from the Blessed Virgin Mary. That same Wednesday night those prayers were answered when the daily signal rockets of Vienna were answered by five rockets from Kahlenberg Hill in the west. Those five brilliant flashes signaled that the relief that Vienna had long-awaited and desperately needed was presently on its way. However, on Thursday, the only banners that waved in the fields around Vienna were the banners of the Ottomans and the soldiers beneath those banners remained in place, not diverted to fight some other foe. Of greatest concern, the cannonades against Vienna slackened, which only ever happened when the Ottomans were preparing a direct attack on the city. That afternoon, with the western horizon still devoid of signs of Christendom, an explosion rocked the western defenses of Vienna when a mine cratered part of Lobl Bastion. Soon after, hundreds of Ottoman soldiers charged up the slope toward Vienna's walls to wrench Lobl Bastion out of the defenders' hands. Starhemberg's expectation of this attack meant that the breach in Lobl's wall had been stuffed with Austrian soldiers. Even after close to sixty days of unending and horrific investment, the Austrians stood strong and drove back the Ottomans twice. The toll that the Austrians inflicted on their attacks was so severe that the Grand Vizier declined sending the third assault. Afterward, Starhemberg quickly organized the repairing and retrenchment of the outer defenses of Vienna. Additionally, Starhemberg backed up these fortifications with chains and barricades in the streets and homes behind the walls. Whether the signals of the day before were true precursors to a timely relief or not, Starhemberg had no intention of surrendering Austria's capital to the enemy. Death was a more palatable alternative. Those signals had not been for naught. A relief army had been formed and was in fact on its way. For the previous two months, just a mere 20,000 Imperial soldiers had remained within touching distance of Vienna to provide the vague suggestion of relief. But over the last weeks of August, that 20,000 men had been dramatically increased to create a real army. First, came 11,000 Bavarians under the personal command of the twenty-one-year-old Elector Maximilian II Emanuel. Unlike any other contingent, even the Emperor's own soldiers, Max Emanuel and his Bavarians had not demanded some incredible subsidy upfront or alternative reward to come to the aid of Vienna. The money could wait until Austria was not in the grips of catastrophe. For now, all Max Emanuel and the Bavarians required was an opportunity to demonstrate their bravery and prove their honor by saving the beleaguered city of Vienna. Shortly after the Bavarians arrived came an army of 6,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry from the Franconian and Swabian Circles. They had only come after weeks of careful negotiation between Emperor Leopold and the Circles, which ended with Emperor Leopold agreeing to pay them a large sum for their services. Next, came 7,000 foot and 2,000 horse of Saxony, who like the Bavarians were commanded by their ruler, Elector Johann Georg IV. While the Bavarians brought with them an impressive train of field artillery, the Saxons brought an essential set of light and mobile artillery pieces. Finally, some smaller units of Germans such as that of Julius Franz of Saxony-Lauenberg added to the army. The last piece of this army was 24,000 Polish footmen and hussars led by King Jan III Sobieski. This eastern army outdid the contribution of any single Imperial prince, even exceeding the army of Emperor Leopold himself. And this number was not even all of it. Some days behind the Poles lagged thousands of the Lithuanian subjects of King Jan III. Bringing this considerable army away from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and then all the way to the Danube had left the Commonwealth itself practically defenseless. In fact, the only defense that King Jan III could offer was a stern warning and a threat of devastating retaliation against the Ottoman partisan Imre Thokoly if he attacked the Commonwealth in the King's absence. However, putting his home in danger was without a doubt necessary to give Christendom a chance to save Vienna. Without the Poles, the Imperial army counted only 50,000 men whereas, with them, the Christians numbered close to 75,000 soldiers. Although this final number was just half that of the Ottomans, it was far better than being only a third. With a King and two Imperial Electors holding commands within this great Christian army, the threat of splintered focus and disorganized tactics was high. Although Emperor Leopold was technically superior to each of them as the Holy Roman Emperor, his previous flight from Vienna had proven that the battlefield was not where his talents lay. Fortunately, the man who Emperor Leopold gave command of his soldiers to, Duke Charles V of Lorraine, proved to be the perfect individual to navigate this multinational army's complicated hierarchy. As the exiled ruler of an occupied duchy Charles of Lorraine's only vocation for the past decade had been being an Imperial general. Through this experience managing the Austrian army's diverse officer corps, Charles of Lorraine learned how to bring an army together around a singular goal through personally connecting with each and every commander of importance. Whereas others were brash and offensive or deferential and meek, Charles of Lorraine was straightforward and easy-going, which was a welcomed ideal among soldiers and commanders alike. Quickly, Charles of Lorraine gained the confidence of the Christian army's generals and bound them to the goal of rescuing Vienna above all else. Under Charles of Lorraine's guidance, Jan Sobieski, Max Emanuel, and Johann Georg all agreed to ignore Emperor Leopold's directive that the relief army should take a longer approach through the gentle grounds to the southwest of Vienna. Instead, in their eagerness to save Vienna, the relief army determined to reach the city as quickly as possible by taking the shortest path across the rocky outcrop of the Wienerwald. With all appropriate haste, the relief army soon cut its way through the forest to Vienna's northwest and then crossed the Danube dangerously close to the Ottoman outriders. By September 8, the army had made its way to Tulln, just 22 miles from Vienna, and was readying its final approach toward Vienna. That night they sent off the signal rockets to inform Vienna of their coming and inspire just a few more days of resistance from the city. When the relief army finally entered the Wienerwald on September 9, it was confronted by an unruly wilderness that had grown out of hand since the Habsburg Emperors had denied the forest to anyone but themselves. As a consequence, the relief army lost its cohesion as it filtered through the forest and up its steep slopes. No man found comfort as he marched or rode through the crowded woods and its sprawling undergrowth, all the while thoughts of a terrible battle hung over him. To make matters worse, a German scouting party spotted Ottomans holding part of the ridgeline in the way of the army's approach. The Ottomans, however, lacked the foresight to either fortify or sufficiently man that ridgeline. This allowed the Christians to pounce on the Ottoman position between dawn on September 11 and wrest control of the ridgeline before the Ottomans could realize their mistake. Yet this victory was not complete as several Ottomans managed to escape from the skirmish and flee back to the main camp where they made the Grand Vizier aware of the relief army's imminent approach. Ottoman scouts had already revealed the relief army to the Grand Vizier two days prior to this attack on the ridge. However, the survivors of the attack were able to confirm the whereabouts of the relief army and its size, which verified the Ottoman belief that the relief army intended to come straight at them from the west and that no attack should be expected from the south where the patrols had still not encountered any Christian soldiers. The narrow geography of the Wienerwald meant that the best avenue for an attack was straight at the center of the Ottoman position. This position could be defended by a series of mannered ridges, hills, and villages. Although the Grand Vizier decided against enhancing the natural defenses provided by the topography with either trenches or palisades, the series of obstacles still presented a formidable challenge. The Christians would have to funnel themselves into multiple zones of fire and if the Ottomans held their ground then it would be a slaughter. Another set of obstacles and an even greater challenge for the Christian army would have to be overcome before they could even reach the Ottoman defenses. After the morning's victory, the Christians were able to occupy the ridge of Kalhenburg and look down toward Vienna. The maps had led them to believe that between that ridge and Vienna lay gentle slopes and clear ploughed fields. Instead, the rocky and uneven ground that had begrudged them in the Wienerwald continued on all the way to the edge of Vienna. The lines that separated the fields were not low wooden fences but haphazard stone walls and thick hedgerows that could not easily be traversed. These demarcations enclosed not open fields of crops but thick and twisted vines of unharvested grapes. Further complicating this approach was a set of deep ravines, small streams, and some scattered villages. Any of these alone was an impediment, but all of them together formed a veritable wall against an assault. As the Christians piloted this difficult terrain they would be easy targets for the Ottoman cannons and muskets. The cavalrymen high up on their horses would be particularly exposed as they slowly negotiated the convoluted ground. All in all, the Christians would have no hope of sending in straight lines of pikemen and musketeers or charging forth coherent blocks of horsemen. Instead, the Christians would have to advance slowly and carefully across the difficult ground and under heavy fire before throwing themselves against prepared defenses and ready defenders. In the face of this adversity, the Christians did not cower. They had come all this way to save Vienna and they would do their damnedest to try, even with so much going against them. However, the Christians' willingness to push on was not the result of confidence or of faith. Many Christian soldiers spent that night sleepless and unable to stomach any food. Even Charles of Lorraine was nervous on the precipice of this battle. They all understood that the likelihood of their victory was low and believed that many of their souls would depart on the morrow. It would be a red day, all they could do was hope it would not be a black day too. On Sunday, September 12, 1683, the great battle for Vienna began when hundreds of Ottoman skirmishers began climbing up the slope toward Kalhenburg and opened fire on the Christian army at around 5 am. With men dropping left and right, the Christians could not hold still and simply return fire. Instead, the Saxon infantrymen abandoned their positions and drove down the hill toward the Ottomans. The whole left flank of the Christian army joined the Saxons in this counterattack that swept away the eastern skirmishers. Although the first Ottoman attack was thrown back, the left flank of the Christian army had placed itself well ahead of the rest of the army in doing so, which left it vulnerable to an Ottoman counterattack. Charles of Lorraine took quick notice of the danger and ordered the left to slow its advance while the rest of the Christian army was ordered to catch up. Although the Saxons had dragged the rest of the army out of its strong positions along the ridge, the earlier success had inspired the men with confidence and even Charles of Lorraine could feel something. The order for a general attack was given. As the Christians crowded around the Ottoman stronghold of Nussberg, they cried out "Ave Maria!" and the Ottomans threw back "Allah, Allah Akbar!" These screams and shouts were drowned out by the overwhelming sound of muskets firing, cannons blasting, and swords clattering. The fighting was vicious and uncertain. But at that particular spot, the Christians found themselves more numerous than the Ottomans and steadily overcame their Ottoman forest. Of great importance were the Saxon light cannons that had been successfully dragged down the slope to directly fire into the Ottoman formations. Within the Ottoman camp, the Grand Vizier was well-aware of the unfolding battle and committed his reserve to saving Nussberg and holding back the Christians. However, the Grand Vizier failed to organize a larger reinforcement from other parts of the army because he could not coordinate with the various pashas and Tatar chiefs. In contrast, even with the dreadful terrain and multinational nature of the army, Charles of Lorraine had maintained decent lines and formations. Close to noon, Johann Georg's cavalry was unleashed on the Ottoman sipahis, which allowed the Saxon infantrymen to wrest Nussberg away from the Ottomans. Still, the Saxons had to fight the Ottomans for each and every house in that village. the continuance of this attack faltered as the Saxons once more overextended themselves in the chase. But once the Christians regrouped they renewed their attack and took the next Ottoman stronghold in front of them. At this point, Charles of Lorraine called for the army to hold to avoid another overextension. He needed to ensure that the army did not lose its cohesion and under the hot summer sun, Charles of Lorraine was worried about his soldiers suffering from exhaustion and thirst. This pause allowed the thousands of Polish cavalry to make their way down the slopes from the Wienerwald and toward the southern edge of the Ottoman position. With the Christian army having successfully made it down the slopes and having already broken one Ottoman position, the Christians finally found themselves at the advantage. Even though the Ottoman army as a whole was larger than the Christian one, on those fields to the west of Vienna, the Christians were superior in number. And now that they had made it down the slope, those numbers could be fully deployed against the Ottomans. Both Charles of Lorraine and Jan Sobieski could feel this shift. To the northeast, Charles of Lorraine asked the German commanders if they wished to push on or whether they should delay the battle to the next day. To the south, Jan Sobieski asked his own commanders the same question. In both councils, the answer was the same: March on. With this order shouted out, the Christians moved forward once again and pushed up to the remaining positions. In the north, the Imperial soldiers led by the Bavarians and Saxons assaulted the Ottoman formations and after an hour and a half, conquered them. All the enemies within them were slaughtered. To the south, the Poles sent a forlorn hope forth to test the Ottoman positions. Although this lonesome company was mauled by the far more numerous Ottomans, their charge still shook the Ottomans just enough for Jan Sobieski to order the entirety of his hussars and the rest of the cavalry to charge the Ottomans. When the Poles bore down on them, the Ottomans did not present themselves as the vicious conquerors of Constantinople. Instead, demoralized by the morning and afternoon's travails, the Ottomans were a disorderly mess that lacked the spirit and discipline necessary to hold against a cavalry charge. The Poles punched through the Ottomans and began to cut them to pieces. Quickly, the Ottomans lost the last of their courage and began to flee. Meanwhile, the Germans to the north continued to stomp over the Ottomans in front of them. Within the hour, the Ottoman army was broken and sent into flight. The citizens of Vienna rejoiced when Charles of Lorraine's official messenger pronounced that "Vienna was relieved". Thousands exited their homes and cried out in jubilation in the streets while others exited the city to set their eyes on their glorious saviours. Everywhere music played and tears of joy and relief painted faces. Although the army remained on alert for the rest of the night in case the Ottomans came back, all knew that no such thing would happen. By some miracle of God, an army of fewer than 75,000 men had secured a true and complete victory over an army of more than 150,000. Vienna was saved and the Ottomans were shattered [1] . While this miracle on the Danube saved Emperor Leopold from suffering the same ignominy of losing Vienna as his ancestor Emperor Frederick III, it was not the only miracle to bless the House of Habsburg on that day. More than a thousand miles away in the heart of Spain at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, another miracle was delivered to the Habsburgs. There, after twelve hours of screaming and crying, Queen Marie Louise of Spain gave birth to the long-awaited first child of King Carlos II of Spain [2] . Better yet, she gave birth to a son who could inherit the many crowns of Spain without any dispute. Thus, Marie Louise ended nearly two decades of uncertainty over who would next possess the crown of Spain. Just as the victory over the Ottomans was celebrated by all within Vienna, the birth of a son, a crown prince, was celebrated by all within Madrid. To them, there could be no greater miracle than that which saved them from a dozen European rulers laying claim to some piece of the Spanish empire once the sickly King Carlos II's heart finally gave out. Thus, both halves of the Habsburg dynasty were saved on the fateful day of September 12, 1683. [1] This is a retelling of the historical relief of Vienna. There is no alteration to make note of. [2] This is the Point of Divergence, Marie Louise produces an heir. There is at least one rumored pregnancy for Marie Louise during her marriage to Carlos II. Unlike the rumored pregnancies of her successor Maria Anna of Neuburg, this rumored pregnancy was taken seriously and not believed to be completely chimerical. One reason for that difference in reactions was that although Carlos II was never conventionally healthy, he was far more relatively healthy while married to Marie Louise. During this time, the only believed issue with conception was his premature ejaculation. Later, when married to Maria Anna, Carlos II was suffering from increasing health issues including atrophy. Here, the suggestion is that Carlos II and Marie Louise manage to get lucky and overcome his premature ejaculation to produce an heir. Alternatively, you are welcome to believe that Marie Louise found another partner. Or even that this is a legitimate miracle from God. Either way, she has produced a child whom Spain will accept as the heir.

If Carlos II of Spain had produced a legitimate surviving son, the most likely immediate result is that the War of the Spanish Succession would not have happened, at least not in the form it did after 1700.

The central problem in real history was that Carlos II died childless, leaving the vast Spanish inheritance contested between the French Bourbons and the Austrian Habsburgs. Spain was weakened, but its empire was still enormous: Spain itself, Spanish America, the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, Naples, Sicily, Sardinia, and other possessions. No major European power wanted either France or Austria to absorb all of that. Carlos’s death therefore created a balance-of-power crisis.

A legitimate son would have solved that crisis. If the boy were recognized as heir, the Spanish monarchy would remain under a Spanish Habsburg line. France would lose its main opportunity to place Philip of Anjou on the Spanish throne, while Austria’s claim through the Habsburg family would become much weaker. England and the Dutch Republic would have far less reason to form a grand coalition against France over Spain. There might still be diplomatic pressure, marriage negotiations, and attempts to influence the Spanish court, but not a general European war over the succession.

Spain itself, however, would not suddenly recover its former greatness. Carlos II’s reign was marked by fiscal weakness, administrative fragmentation, aristocratic factionalism, and dependence on foreign diplomacy. If his son were a minor when Carlos died, Spain would likely be governed by a regency dominated by court factions, grandees, clerics, and foreign ambassadors. France and Austria would compete for influence over the young king, but through diplomacy rather than open partition.

The biggest long-term difference is that Spain would probably avoid the Bourbon reforms of the eighteenth century. In real history, the Bourbon victory brought a more centralized monarchy, the abolition of many Aragonese and Catalan privileges after the war, administrative restructuring, and later attempts to modernize the empire. A surviving Habsburg heir would likely preserve more of the older composite monarchy: Castile, Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, and the overseas empire retaining more traditional institutions. That could mean less internal trauma, but also slower reform.

Europe would also look different. Britain might not gain Gibraltar and Minorca in 1704–1713, because those gains came out of the War of the Spanish Succession. The Treaty of Utrecht would not reshape Europe in the same way. Austria might not receive the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, Naples, and Sardinia. Savoy might not rise as quickly in status. France, spared the enormous cost of the succession war, could remain financially and militarily stronger in the early eighteenth century, though still burdened by earlier wars and structural fiscal problems.

The Spanish Empire in the Americas would probably remain intact for longer under Habsburg rule, but not necessarily stronger. Without Bourbon administrative and commercial reforms, colonial government might remain looser and more corporatist. That could delay some tensions that later contributed to independence movements, but it might also leave Spain less able to extract revenue or defend its empire against Britain and other rivals.

The outcome depends heavily on the son’s health and age. If Carlos II’s son were sickly, childless, or died young, Europe could simply face the same succession crisis a generation later. If he survived, married well, and had children, the Spanish Habsburg dynasty could continue, and the great Bourbon-Habsburg confrontation over Spain would be avoided.

So the most plausible answer is: Carlos II having a son would probably prevent the War of the Spanish Succession, keep the Spanish Empire formally intact under a Spanish Habsburg dynasty, and delay or prevent Bourbon centralization. But it would not restore Spain to sixteenth-century dominance. Spain would likely remain a great but weakened imperial monarchy, preserved by legitimacy rather than revived by strength.

Assuming this means an Alternate History Challenge to create the most successful plausible George W. Bush presidency, the easiest “wank” is not to make Bush a genius or a liberal, but to give him better advisers and remove the Iraq War.

The point of divergence should be in 2000–2001: Bush chooses a more realist, less Cheney/Rumsfeld-dominated foreign-policy team. Cheney either is not vice president or is kept from becoming the central power in the administration; someone like John Danforth, George Voinovich, or even Colin Powell fills the moderating elder-statesman role. Defense goes to a cautious realist such as Robert Gates or Brent Scowcroft’s circle rather than Rumsfeld. Bush still governs as a conservative Republican, but his “CEO president” style now delegates to people less interested in Iraq, executive secrecy, and transformational war.

The crucial change is after 9/11. Bush responds forcefully but narrowly: Afghanistan, al-Qaeda, and the Taliban, not Iraq. At Tora Bora, he commits U.S. troops instead of relying heavily on Afghan proxies and Pakistani cooperation, making it much more plausible that bin Laden is killed or captured in late 2001. The Taliban regime still falls, but the U.S. does not then divert attention, troops, intelligence assets, and diplomatic capital to Iraq. Afghanistan receives a larger stabilization effort, NATO support remains stronger, and Pakistan is pressured more seriously over Taliban sanctuaries. The war is still messy, but it is not drowned by a second, elective war.

Bush also avoids the worst “war on terror” mistakes. No Abu Ghraib scandal, no Iraq WMD humiliation, no massive Guantanamo/torture controversy, or at least much less of it. The Patriot Act still passes, but the administration behaves more like a post-9/11 Eisenhower/Nixon realist security state than a crusading neoconservative one. International sympathy after 9/11 remains largely intact. France, Germany, and Canada may grumble about Afghanistan, but there is no global rupture over Iraq.

Domestically, Bush’s “compassionate conservatism” becomes more than branding. He still passes tax cuts, but they are smaller, more middle-class-focused, and more tied to economic conditions. Without Iraq, the deficit problem is much less severe. No Iraq War also frees political capital for immigration reform, which Bush genuinely favored. A Bush-McCain-Kennedy-style immigration bill could plausibly pass around 2005, especially if Bush’s approval remains high after a successful Afghanistan/bin Laden outcome.

No Child Left Behind is better funded and less punitive. Medicare Part D still passes, but with stronger cost controls or partial pay-fors. Bush’s faith-based initiatives remain controversial but not presidency-defining. Social Security privatization is either dropped early or reframed as a small voluntary savings add-on rather than a doomed major reform.

Katrina is another major fix. Bush appoints a competent FEMA head instead of Michael Brown, treats the storm as a national-security-scale crisis, prepositions federal resources, and visits decisively. New Orleans still suffers, but the image of indifference and incompetence never forms. This alone preserves much of his second-term legitimacy.

The 2008 financial crisis is harder to eliminate, because the housing bubble had deep roots in the Fed, Wall Street, Congress, global savings flows, and decades of mortgage policy. But a “wanked” Bush can soften it. After Enron and WorldCom, he backs tougher financial regulation, stronger mortgage-lending standards, and earlier oversight of derivatives and investment-bank leverage. The housing bubble still grows, but less grotesquely. Instead of a catastrophic 2008 collapse, the U.S. gets a serious recession in 2007–2008 that is handled with earlier bank recapitalization and mortgage relief. Bush leaves office damaged by the economy, but not historically discredited.

In this timeline, Bush wins reelection in 2004 comfortably, perhaps by a larger margin than in real life. Republicans may still lose seats in 2006 because of normal sixth-year fatigue, but there is no Iraq disaster dragging them down. The GOP remains more internationalist, more pro-immigration, and less conspiratorial. A Republican such as McCain, Romney, or even Jeb Bush has a much better chance in 2008, especially if the financial crisis is milder.

Bush’s legacy in this best plausible version is not “one of the greatest presidents,” because he still presides over 9/11, expands executive power, cuts taxes heavily, and governs in a polarized era. But he could plausibly be remembered as a successful conservative wartime president: the man who destroyed al-Qaeda’s Afghan base, captured or killed bin Laden early, avoided the Iraq quagmire, passed education and Medicare reforms, handled immigration constructively, and left office with moderate approval rather than as a cautionary tale.

The shortest version: for a wanked Bush presidency, remove Cheney/Rumsfeld dominance, capture bin Laden at Tora Bora, do not invade Iraq, handle Katrina competently, and regulate the housing/financial sector earlier. That gives Bush a credible path to being remembered as a solid or even near-great Republican president rather than one of the most controversial modern presidents.

items.original_question: What if Umar ibn Hafsun defeats the Umayyads - Mozarab/Muladí Al-Andalus One of my favorite historical subjects to research is Al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled realms of the Iberian peninsula that existed between the 8th and 15th centuries. A land where East met West, Al-Andalus represented a rare example of Islamic Arab rule of Western European territory, resulting in the blending of cultures, religion, knowledge, and languages that proved to be massively influential on the development of European civilization and human history as a whole. Even though it was swept out of Iberia by the Reconquista, the influence of Al-Andalus can still be felt today, through Hispanic language, culture, art, and cuisine. For example, there are many Arabic loanwords in the Spanish language, tacos have middle eastern roots, and I remember a story my grandfather would tell me about when he met Bedouin tribesmen while deployed as a U.S. Marine during the Gulf War, and while they could not understand the English language, they could understand his Spanish. In the late 9th century, the once-Caliphs of the entire Muslim world, the Arab Umayyad dynasty, ruled over the vast majority of the Iberian peninsula from the prosperous city of Cordoba. Their rule would last for 300 years, but would not be without resistance. Although they comprised a small portion of the population, the ruling class of Al-Andalus was almost exclusively Arab. Mozarabs, local Iberians who remained Christian under Muslim rule, and Muladí, Iberians who had converted to Islam, resented the discriminatory racial and taxation policies of their Arab overlords, creating a degree of instability within Al-Andalus. Born around 850, Umar ibn Hafsun was a prominent leader of Iberian resistance to Umayyad rule. Simultaneously described as being of both North African and Visigothic descent, the rogue-ish and opportunistic ibn Hafsun attracted a following of disaffected Mozarab and Muladí alike, and alongside fellow rebels such as ibn Marwan and the Banu Qasi clan, would contest Umayyad rule from his fortress, Bobastro. While he would experience much success early on, several defeats against the Umayyads, such as at the Battle of Poley in 891, as well as his conversion to Christianity in 899, in what appeared to be a bid to attract the support of the Christian King of Asturias, would weaken his following. He would fight to the very end, dying in 917, and his sons would continue his fight until 928, when Bobastro fell to Emir Abd-ar-Rahman III. Umar ibn Hafsun remains somewhat of a tragic figure in Iberian history, but he also represents a glimpse into what could have been. Had he succeeded in supplanting the minority Arab ruling class with Mozarabs and Muladí, perhaps by winning battles such as the Battle of Poley, ibn Hafsun could have ensured the creation of a stronger, multicultural and multireligious Al-Andalus. This creates an interesting scenario for speculation. Could this alt-Andalus survive for longer, perhaps even to the present? What would the society of alt-Andalus look like? Would religious and ethnic differences eventually shatter this state, or would it strengthen it, combining the best of the Christian and Islamic worlds? Would alt-Andalus fall to neighboring Christian and Muslim invaders, or would it become one of the leading powers in Europe and the Mediterranean, an even greater conduit for the exchange of trade, knowledge, and culture than the Al-Andalus of OTL? And how would this alt-Andalus impact the development of Hispanic culture, and European and world history as a whole?

If Umar ibn Hafsun had decisively defeated the Umayyads of Córdoba, the most likely result would not have been a stable “Mozarab/Muladí Al-Andalus” in the modern national sense. It would more likely have been an earlier collapse of centralized Umayyad rule and the emergence of a fragmented Andalusi order dominated by local converts, Mozarab Christian communities, Berber chiefs, and regional strongmen.

Umar ibn Hafsun’s rebellion was powerful because it united many groups alienated from the Cordoban emirate: Muladíes, meaning local Iberian converts to Islam; Mozarabs, Christians living under Muslim rule; Berbers; and disaffected Arab and provincial elites. His base at Bobastro became the center of a broad anti-Umayyad movement. But that coalition was held together mainly by opposition to Córdoba, not by a shared political program. If he had taken Córdoba or destroyed Umayyad authority before the rise of Abd al-Rahman III, he would have faced the hard problem of turning a rebellion into a state.

A victorious Ibn Hafsun would probably have tried to rule as a local Andalusi alternative to the Arab Umayyad elite. At first, he may have presented himself as a Muslim ruler defending the rights of non-Arab converts and provincial communities. That would have appealed to many Muladíes, who resented Arab aristocratic privilege. But his later conversion, or re-conversion, to Christianity would have made a unified rule over Muslim-majority regions much harder. If he openly ruled as a Christian, many Muslim allies would likely desert him, and rival Islamic leaders in Seville, Córdoba, Zaragoza, Toledo, or the frontier zones would claim legitimacy against him.

So the most plausible outcome is an Al-Andalus that breaks apart a century earlier than it did historically. Instead of the strong 10th-century Caliphate of Córdoba under Abd al-Rahman III and al-Hakam II, Iberia would see something resembling the later taifa period much sooner: Córdoba weakened, regional dynasties emerging, frontier cities acting independently, and Christian northern kingdoms finding more room to intervene.

For the Mozarabs, the short-term result would likely be favorable. Christian communities in the south would gain more political protection, churches could become more visible, and Mozarab elites might enter government in greater numbers. Bobastro or another southern center could become the capital of a hybrid Andalusi Christian-Muslim polity, using Arabic administration but drawing legitimacy from local Iberian and Christian support. This would not mean the disappearance of Islam from al-Andalus. Islam was already deeply rooted, especially in cities and among converted local families. Arabic culture, Islamic law, and Muslim urban elites would remain powerful.

For the Muladíes, an Ibn Hafsun victory would be even more important. It could elevate local Iberian Muslim converts over the old Arab lineages. Al-Andalus might become less “Umayyad Arab” and more “native Andalusi,” with power shifting to rural lords, converted families, and regional military elites. In cultural terms, Arabic would probably still dominate government and high culture, while Romance dialects would remain widely spoken among Christians and many rural communities.

The northern Christian kingdoms—Asturias/León, Navarre, and later Castile—would benefit from the weakening of Córdoba. Without Abd al-Rahman III’s strong caliphate, they would face less pressure from the south. Their expansion into the Duero valley and beyond could happen faster. But they would not necessarily conquer all of al-Andalus quickly. A Mozarab/Muladí southern state might ally with León or Navarre when useful, but it would also resist northern domination. It would be culturally Andalusi, not simply an extension of the northern Christian kingdoms.

The wider Islamic world would also react. The Fatimids in North Africa, rising around the same period, would likely see a weakened al-Andalus as an opportunity. Historically, the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba became a major rival to the Fatimids. If the Umayyads collapsed, Fatimid influence in the western Mediterranean might grow much stronger. Some Andalusi Muslim rulers might even invite Fatimid support against Ibn Hafsun or his successors.

The biggest cultural consequence would be the absence, or severe weakening, of the Cordoban golden age. Without the Umayyad restoration under Abd al-Rahman III, Córdoba probably would not become the same great caliphal capital. The massive court culture, libraries, diplomacy, architecture, and administrative sophistication of 10th-century Córdoba would either not develop or would be dispersed among several smaller courts. Al-Andalus would remain culturally rich, but less centralized and less internationally powerful.

In the long term, Ibn Hafsun’s victory would probably produce a more religiously mixed but politically unstable Iberia. A durable Mozarab/Muladí kingdom is possible, especially in the mountainous south around Málaga and Ronda, but ruling all of al-Andalus from such a base would be difficult. His coalition was too divided, and his legitimacy too contested. The more likely result is an early taifa-like fragmentation, faster Christian expansion in the north, stronger Fatimid pressure from Africa, and no powerful Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba.

So, in direct terms: if Umar ibn Hafsun defeated the Umayyads, al-Andalus would become less Arab-Umayyad and more locally Iberian, with greater power for Muladíes and Mozarabs. But it would probably not become a unified Christian-Mozarab state. It would become a fractured, hybrid Andalusi world where Islam, Christianity, Arabic culture, and local Iberian identities competed much earlier and more openly than they did in actual history.

A plausible best-case alternate timeline would look like this:

**1. Late Roman Empire: Christianity becomes influential but not coercive.**  
After Constantine, the Church gains legal protection and public influence, but avoids becoming too dependent on imperial power. It condemns forced conversion, antisemitic violence, and religious persecution much earlier. This gives Catholicism moral authority without tying it too closely to state coercion.

**2. Early councils: Eastern divisions are avoided.**  
The disputes after the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon are handled with better diplomacy and language. The Oriental Orthodox churches—Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, and others—remain in communion with Rome and Constantinople. Christianity remains much more united across the Mediterranean, Middle East, and Africa.

**3. The East–West Schism never becomes permanent.**  
In the 11th century, Rome and Constantinople reach a compromise: the pope is recognized as having a real primacy, but within a more synodal structure that respects the Eastern patriarchs. The *Filioque* dispute is resolved by allowing different liturgical expressions without declaring the other side heretical. No permanent Catholic–Orthodox split occurs.

**4. The Crusades are more restrained and less destructive.**  
The First Crusade may still happen as a response to Byzantine appeals and Muslim-Turkish expansion, but the papacy imposes stricter discipline. There is no massacre of Jerusalem, no Fourth Crusade, and no sack of Constantinople. Relations with Jews, Muslims, and Eastern Christians remain far better. Catholicism avoids one of the greatest stains on its historical reputation.

**5. Medieval reform succeeds earlier.**  
The Church cracks down sooner on simony, corrupt bishops, absentee clergy, and the sale of indulgences. Monastic and scholastic renewal still happen, but reform becomes continuous rather than crisis-driven. Universities flourish under Church patronage, and Catholicism becomes even more strongly associated with learning, law, medicine, philosophy, and science.

**6. The Protestant Reformation becomes an internal Catholic reform movement.**  
By the early 1500s, the papacy recognizes the seriousness of corruption and calls a major reform council before Luther’s break becomes irreversible. Indulgence abuses are abolished, Scripture and preaching in vernacular languages are encouraged, clerical education is improved, and bishops are required to live in their dioceses. Luther, Erasmus, and other reformers remain within the Church as controversial but influential reform voices. There is no permanent Catholic–Protestant split, or at least it is much smaller.

**7. Colonial missions defend indigenous peoples consistently.**  
The papacy enforces its anti-slavery and pro-indigenous teachings much more aggressively. Catholic monarchs are threatened with excommunication for enslavement, forced conversion, and exploitation. Missionaries still evangelize in the Americas, Africa, and Asia, but with stronger protection for native languages, cultures, and legal rights. Catholicism becomes associated less with empire and more with anti-colonial defense of human dignity.

**8. Science and modernity are handled better.**  
The Galileo affair is avoided or resolved quietly. Catholic universities become major centers of astronomy, biology, medicine, and physics. In the 18th and 19th centuries, the Church opposes atheistic materialism but accepts constitutional government, religious liberty, and modern science earlier. This prevents the long image of Catholicism as reactionary or anti-modern.

**9. The Church responds to democracy and human rights earlier.**  
Instead of fighting liberalism broadly, the papacy distinguishes between anti-Christian secularism and legitimate civil freedoms. Catholic social teaching develops earlier: workers’ rights, limits on capitalism, defense of the poor, opposition to racism, and protection of families. The Church becomes the strongest global moral voice against both totalitarianism and economic exploitation.

**10. The abuse crisis is prevented or confronted immediately.**  
In the 20th century, bishops adopt strict global standards for child protection, transparency, and removal of abusive clergy. Cover-ups are punished severely. This preserves much more trust in the priesthood and Church institutions.

In this best timeline, Catholicism remains recognizably Catholic: sacramental, apostolic, liturgical, Marian, episcopal, and centered on communion with Rome. But it is less imperial, less defensive, more synodal, more intellectually confident, and more morally consistent.

The result would likely be a much larger and more unified global Church. Catholicism might include most of what are now Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, and many Protestant communities. Europe would be less religiously fractured, Latin America and Africa would have a less colonial Catholic memory, and the Church’s public reputation would be far stronger.

So the “best timeline” for Catholicism is not one where it wins every political battle. It is one where it avoids the major schisms, reforms before crises explode, rejects coercion and corruption earlier, protects the vulnerable more consistently, and becomes the most trusted global institution for faith, learning, charity, and human dignity.

Assuming you mean Princess Mary Tudor, daughter of Henry VIII and later Mary I of England: if she had married Philip of Bavaria in the late 1530s or early 1540s, the biggest change would be that Mary’s reign would probably not have been tied to Spain.

Philip of Bavaria was a Wittelsbach prince, far less powerful than Philip of Spain. A marriage to him would have given Mary a respectable Catholic husband and a continental connection, but not the overwhelming Habsburg alliance that later alarmed many English nobles. As a result, if Mary still became queen in 1553, there likely would have been less fear that England was becoming a Spanish dependency. The Wyatt Rebellion, which was driven largely by opposition to Mary’s Spanish marriage, might not have happened or would have been much weaker.

The most important question is whether Mary and Philip had children. If they had a surviving child, especially a son, Elizabeth’s later succession would probably be blocked. England might then have had a Catholic Tudor-Wittelsbach line after Mary, making the Elizabethan Protestant settlement far less likely. England could have remained officially Catholic longer, though Protestant resistance would still have been strong.

If Mary had no surviving children, the outcome changes less dramatically. Philip of Bavaria died in 1548, before Mary became queen, so Mary might have come to the throne as a widow. In that case she probably still would have tried to restore Catholicism, but without the unpopular Spanish marriage her regime might have looked more English and less foreign. England also might have avoided being drawn into the Habsburg-Valois war, meaning the loss of Calais in 1558 might not have happened.

So the likely result is: a less Spanish, somewhat less unpopular Mary Tudor regime; possibly no Wyatt Rebellion; possibly no loss of Calais; and, if Mary had a surviving child by Philip of Bavaria, no Elizabeth I and a much stronger chance of a continued Catholic monarchy in England.

human_answers: I suppose the first question is what is meant by apocrypha? Because it can mean different things and they're all different to address. Is it what many Protestants and Rabbinic Judaism call apocrypha? That is the additional books of the Old Testament that are instead considered Deuterocanon in Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy? At its core, these are books found in the LXX (Septuagint), but not found in the Masoretic text and are considered canonical texts for the majority of the Christian world. Removing the Protestant Masoretic preference resolves that part easily. Is it the broader Second Temple literature, often called Jewish Apocrypha? This is largely apocalyptic literature and includes things like Enoch, the somewhat related Jubilees, Esdras A (or III Ezra, or I Esdras...) , the Apocalypse of Esdra (IV Ezra/II Esdras), the various Baruchs, but also includes Wisdom literature like Psalms 151-155, Wisdom of Sirach, and the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs. Some of these were contained in LXX translations (Sirach, the Esdras, Psalms 151-155, etc), while others weren't (Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, II Baruch, Enoch). This is a mixed bag for canonical status, some of them made it in due to being in existing Greek collections (the LXX), while others weren't. Enoch certainly saw a lot of respect in the early church, but it ultimately lost its status over time and only remained in Ethiopia; which itself has weird canon, the Ethiopic Bible includes Enoch and Jubilees before the Esdras, and also includes the 3 Books of Meqabyan (Ethiopic Maccabees), while disincluding the actual Books of Maccabees (and the Ethiopic books are not at all related, they aren't about martyrs at all in fact, and are almost certainly written in the Middle Ages in Ge'ez originally). A lot of these are interesting books that could have significant impact on theology, but most of them are written quite late too, which was a large part of why they weren't included in any canon; most were know pseudepigrapha even at the time. Then we have the New Testament apocrypha, which ranges from things like gnostic literature and known pseudepigrapha with little chance of incorporation to the antilegomena, many of which had good chance of inclusion. Those not included, but that could have been are the Gospel of the Hebrews (scholars think there's actually 3 different works under this title, and they're all lost), the Apocalypse of Peter, the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle of Barnabas and the Didache. Worth stating is that the antilegomena weren't "removed," there was heavy debate early in Christianity of what was and wasn't canonical. Different churches used different books. Some were popular in one place, but unknown in others. Worth stating for the record: the Council of Nicea had NOTHING to do with canonical formation and this was still getting discussed for centuries after. The Church Father Jerome is one of the most important figures in the Old Testament canon development, he was highly influential in the West and was one of the main reasons for why the Catholic and Orthodox Deuterocanons are slightly different. As far as the New Testament, most of the Acts of the Apostyles genre were known pseudepigrapha and very clearly non-canonical even in content. They were popular literature and very clearly derived from the Greek novel tradition. Acts of Paul being one exception to this, it was deeply popular and some argued canonical, but in a canon that includes the Pastorals (and even the Deutero-Paulines), it just didn't fit with the theology of the Pauline letters (although I'd argue it fits quite well with the Authentic Pauline corpus). The Apocylpse of Peter wasn't actually well regarded by most priests and theologians though, but it was certainly popular. Its essentially an early Dante's Inferno. The Shepherd/Hermas, Barnabas (NOT the Gospel of Barnabas, which is a medieval forgery), and the Didache I think are the easiest bunch, although not entirely without problem. The Shepherd is deeply allegorical, but was known to not be apostolic (not insurmountable, as Hebrews made it in, but apostolic lineage was important) and has an arguably binitarian lean to it. Barnabas is also allegorical and also deeply anti-jewish. It is essentially saying that the Jews misread their own books, and this is what the Jewish laws really mean - a lot of these require some serious contortion, to say the least. The Didache is interesting since its the first book of the genre of "Church Orders," which are basically moral and litergical texts. In some ways, its an early version of the genre that would become the Anglican Book of Common Prayer. Some other possibilities are the Odes of Solomon, which are a Judeo-Christian work, likely from the Qumran community, with a pretty strong connection to the Johannine literature.

Another work to consider is the Ascension of Isaiah, a christian work written as a series of visions/prophecies of the prophet Isaiah. Also, the Book of Adam and Eve could become part of the Bible, it discusses what happens to Adam and Eve after Genesis, which is interesting. I doubt the distinction of a so-called "Thomasine" branch of anything, seeing as the gospel of Thomas is a late forgery, dating from the 2nd Century, and not originating from any known centers of Christianity claiming Thomasine origin, Kerala, Edessa or Bactria. The chance of the Didache becoming part of the Bible seems slight to me, seeing as its genre isnt really saying it should be, its just a how to book, thought to be directed to clergy. I would agree the best chance to expand is going to be the Apostolic fathers works: Letters of Ignatius, Polycarp, possibly Papias' work might make it in as a supplement to Acts of the Apostles.

Something to keep in mind, is that "canon" actually has different meanings. And what you mean by "canon" could have major implications on just how big it can get. To general Protestants, the Biblical Canon means that these are only 66 divinely inspired books, period, no more, no less (the familiar Protestant Canon). The Catholic teaching is a bit more nuanced. It states that there are at least 73 divinely inspired books (which make up the Catholic Canon). This does actual leave open the possibility that there are other books that could be divinely inspire but just are not included. That said, there are some individual books that have been rule as incompatible with canon & not divinely inspired. For most of the other Christian sects, the concept of canon is a bit "fuzzier." With many of the books falling into a category that could best be described as "potentially divinely inspired, but since it we see no problems with it we don't need to bother making any further determinations". Thus they are still included in the canon list.

items.original_question:
AHC: Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible

The definition of "apocrypha" obviously varies across denomination, e.g. 1 Enoch is canon according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church but not any other major denominations. But I'm thinking more along the lines of having some denomination which recognizes as many texts as possible which are not in every Biblical canon IOTL (and possible none), e.g. Acts of various specific figures (as distinct from Acts of the Apostles), Gospel of Thomas, etc. etc.
items.model_answer:
A Christian or post-Christian religion that incorporated as many “apocrypha” as possible would probably become a very broad, eclectic, and internally tension-filled tradition rather than simply “Christianity with extra books.”

The closest real-world precedent is the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose biblical canon is already much larger than most Christian canons and includes books such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, 1–3 Meqabyan, and others. A maximal apocryphal canon would go much further: it might include the Deuterocanonical books, Jewish pseudepigrapha, Enochic literature, Jubilees, Testament literature, apocryphal gospels, infancy gospels, apocryphal acts of apostles, apocalypses, Nag Hammadi texts, works like the Shepherd of Hermas, the Didache, 1 Clement, the Epistle of Barnabas, the Apocalypse of Peter, the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Peter, the Protoevangelium of James, the Acts of Paul and Thecla, and many others.

The main result would be a religion with a much larger and stranger sacred history. Angels, demons, cosmic rebellion, hidden heavenly journeys, the fall of the Watchers, and elaborate apocalyptic geography would become far more central because of texts like 1 Enoch and related literature. Mary, Joseph, James, Thomas, Thecla, and other figures would receive much more attention. Jesus’ childhood, post-resurrection appearances, secret teachings, and descent into the underworld would be expanded in ways that are only marginal or absent in the standard New Testament. The religion would likely have a richer mythological and visionary imagination than mainstream Catholic, Orthodox, or Protestant Christianity.

But the biggest problem would be contradiction. Many apocryphal texts do not agree with each other or with the canonical Bible. Some are broadly orthodox. Some are Jewish apocalyptic. Some are ascetic. Some are proto-Gnostic or fully Gnostic. Some imply a creator-God or demiurge distinct from the highest God. Some present Jesus as more human, others as more purely divine or visionary. Some promote celibacy and rejection of ordinary family life; others expand family-centered piety. A church that treated all these writings as equally authoritative and literally true would have a difficult time maintaining a coherent doctrine.

So such a religion would almost certainly need a layered canon. It might say: the traditional Bible is the “primary canon,” the apocrypha are “secondary canon,” and the more esoteric or contradictory writings are “mystical” or “allegorical” scripture. Without that hierarchy, the tradition would fragment quickly. With it, the religion could survive as a post-Christian “great library” tradition: not based on one tight creed, but on a vast sacred archive interpreted through ritual, allegory, and spiritual discipline.

Doctrinally, it would probably move away from strict Protestant-style biblical authority. A maximal apocryphal church would need priests, teachers, councils, or mystagogues to decide how to interpret the mass of texts. It would be closer to Eastern Orthodoxy, Ethiopian Christianity, esoteric Christianity, or even some forms of Gnosticism than to Reformation Christianity. Tradition would become more important, not less, because scripture would be too large and diverse to interpret plainly.

In worship and practice, it might emphasize angels, saints, visionary ascent, fasting, ritual purity, sacred names, apocalyptic expectation, and hidden wisdom. Thecla and other female holy figures could become especially important. Mary might become even more central because texts like the Protoevangelium of James greatly expand her sacred biography. Enoch might be treated almost like a primordial prophet. Thomasine or Gnostic-leaning communities might emphasize inner enlightenment and secret sayings of Jesus.

Mainstream Christians would likely regard this religion as heterodox or heretical, especially if it canonized Gnostic gospels or texts that contradict Nicene doctrine. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant churches historically excluded many of these writings precisely because they were late, pseudonymous, doctrinally suspect, or not widely used in public worship. A maximal apocryphal canon would therefore define the group as standing outside ordinary Christian orthodoxy, unless it carefully subordinated the problematic books to the traditional canon.

In short, a Christian or post-Christian religion that canonized as many apocrypha as possible would be expansive, mystical, apocalyptic, and diverse, but also unstable unless it created a strong interpretive hierarchy. If it treated every text equally, it would collapse into contradiction. If it treated the apocrypha as a vast secondary sacred library, it could become a coherent esoteric or post-Christian tradition: a Christianity of many gospels, many apocalypses, many apostolic legends, and many layers of hidden meaning.

human_answers: "What factors allowed the European powers to accept native princes in Serbia" is a false question because it presumes the European powers had a role in allowing native princes there to begin with. With the exception of Russia during the First Serbian Uprising, there were no other powers involved beyond the Ottomans. Had it ended with the First Serbian Uprising, whether in Ičko's Peace in 1807 or by 1813 otherwise, we would've seen the Ottomans consenting to a native prince in the region, in the form of Karađorđe, by themselves, and that'd be the end of it. Karađorđe was already attempting to consolidate power for himself in those latter years, even while he had opposition, so he was already set to be uncontested. Which brings forth two questions: had the Greeks fought alone, would it have increased the odds of a native prince being put in power, and would they have even chosen to be a monarchy? As others have argued so far, there was too much conflict between the various revolutionaries to allow for something like that, and it's also why OTL there actually wasn't a monarchy in Greece after the revolution until Greece's stability was brought under question and it was decided by the Great Powers that it should be a monarchy with a foreign prince in power to bolster it. This ignores some of the historical facts surrounding the dynastic conflict in Serbia. Obrenović didn't just decide he was going to challenge Karađorđe's claim to authority over the Serbs, he had become a leader in his own right, rallied the people to another uprising, and won, by the time Karađorđe attempted to come back. He had received what Karađorđe would've gotten had the First Serbian Uprising won, effectively, and he wasn't going to let him challenge that, least of all because of fears of what the Ottomans might do in response. Had the Greek War of Independence seen a decisively unifying leader like Karađorđe or Obrenović from its outset, there's no reason to assume that you'd have other leaders contesting their claim to power by wishing to assert themselves instead - when Karađorđe attempted to consolidate power, he received pushback on it, and it's likely a Greek-equivalent situation would see a similar conflict, where the consolidating leader would receive pushback from his revolutionary peers. But as everyone else has pointed out, revolutionary leadership was a lot more diffuse and filled with conflict, so there's no chance you'd have a unifying leader like that emerge. Really, the case of Serbia should highlight the fact that, had the Greek War of Independence not been a war for independence, but a war for greater autonomy ala the First Serbian Uprising up to 1807, in a TL where it was successful, depending on who's Sultan at the time, the same privileges extended in Ičko's Peace to the Serbs might be extended to the Greeks too, which means that the Ottomans would've demanded the Greeks decide on who to be prince among their leaders.

AHC: Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek

Greece became independent from the Ottoman Empire in 1821. Two different European dynasties ruled it - the Bavarians (whose only king of Greece was the unpopular King Otto) and the Danish. Neither of these dynasties were of Greek heritage. However, there was a sizable Greek aristocracy in the Ottoman Empire, such as the Phanariotes of Constantinople. What if an ethnically Greek family (such as one of the Phanariot families) was chosen to rule Greece? Can you think of some candidates for a possible ethnically Greek royal family for 19th century Greece?
items.model_answer:
If Greece had had an ethnically Greek royal family instead of the Bavarian Wittelsbachs and later the Danish Glücksburgs, the monarchy probably would have had somewhat stronger symbolic legitimacy, but it would not necessarily have made Greek politics stable or ensured the survival of the monarchy.

After independence, the Great Powers chose foreign princes partly because a local Greek dynasty might have favored one faction, clan, region, or military network over others. A Greek royal family—perhaps from a prominent Phanariot, island, or revolutionary family—would have seemed more “national” and could have avoided the recurring criticism that the monarchy was foreign. This might have helped the crown connect better with Greek nationalism, Orthodoxy, language, and popular memory of the War of Independence.

However, the main problems of the Greek monarchy were not only ethnic. Greece faced chronic issues: dependence on Britain, France, and Russia; weak institutions; military intervention in politics; the Megali Idea and territorial expansion; economic instability; the National Schism between royalists and Venizelists; defeat in Asia Minor; republicanism; dictatorship; and Cold War polarization. An ethnically Greek dynasty would still have had to navigate these same crises.

A Greek royal house might have changed a few things. It could have reduced resentment toward “foreign kings,” especially in the 19th century. It might have made the monarchy more acceptable to nationalist officers and the Orthodox Church. It may also have limited the cultural distance seen under King Otto, whose Bavarian entourage and Catholic background alienated many Greeks. If the dynasty were Orthodox, Greek-speaking, and tied to the independence struggle, it would likely have been harder to portray as alien.

But there would also have been risks. A native dynasty might have been seen as the victory of one Greek faction over others. Families from the Peloponnese, the islands, Phanariot circles, or military elites all had rivals. Instead of being a neutral foreign compromise, a Greek king could have deepened internal competition. The Great Powers might also have distrusted a native dynasty as more likely to pursue aggressive nationalist policies, especially toward Ottoman lands.

The biggest possible difference would be in legitimacy during crises. During moments like the 1862 overthrow of Otto, the National Schism, or the republican movements of the 1920s and 1970s, an ethnically Greek monarchy might have had a better chance of surviving public anger. But if it still opposed popular governments, mishandled wars, or aligned with unpopular foreign interests, ethnicity alone would not save it.

So the most likely outcome is: a Greek ethnic royal family would have made the monarchy feel more authentically national and might have delayed or softened anti-monarchist sentiment, but it would not automatically have prevented coups, republics, or eventual abolition. The survival of the Greek monarchy would have depended less on ancestry and more on whether the crown accepted constitutional limits, avoided partisan conflict, and adapted to modern democratic politics.
