Heiresses in weak negotiating positions often lost everything to their husbands and, considering both that a) Elizabeth de Burgh only became an heiress because her father was assassinated by his cousin -- i.e., the man who would inherit if Elizabeth did not -- and b) that Elizabeth's guardian was her mother, Maud of Lancaster, who was a member of the English royal family herself, it just seems very likely that the marriage contract gave Lionel everything. Maud was predisposed to favor the royal family as a relative herself and would be very strongly predisposed to screw over the Burghs who murdered her husband by disinheriting them in favor of Lionel.

To be fair, when the negotiations presumably happen (1366 or 1367 the latest) Philippa's father Lionel is alive, healthy and about to be married for the second time. I don’t think the perspective of Philippa inheriting his estates looks all that close at this point. Moreover, I don’t think that the perspective of Pedro potentially inheriting domains in England and Ireland should scare Edward all that much. If anything, they could potentially serve as a hook to ensure the favorable Castilian policy towards England or otherwise they can be easily confiscated (it’s not like Castile can really try retain those estates against the wishes of Plantagenets). If after Lionel dies Edward really wants to revert these estates back to the crown (although as mentioned before there are arguments for Edward not to do it), I think there is a really neat way to do it. Presumably Philippa’s dowry however large can it be (BTW how large can it be? Up to £10,000 perhaps?) would not be enough to pay for Black Prince’s army (even if ITTL Edward, helping the future husband of his niece, can be a bit more moderate in his pricing). While Pedro can raise some money on his own (he was ready to pay de Guesclin 200000 gold coins – presumably florins - in 1369, so he had some money, although of course it wouldn’t be enough to settle his OTL bill with Edward), he would probably still need to pledge some his territories in lieu of the rest of the payment. So, after Philippa inherits her father’s estates, the mortgage can be rearranged with English and Irish estates now serving as a collateral instead of Castilian territories. Or even perhaps these estates can be given to the Black Prince staight away in lieu of the rest of the debt. @material_boy , what do you think about the proposed PoD and some of its consequences? I have been toying with the victorious Pedro for several years now, but the perspective of modeling the alternative HYW always seemed to daunting. It was your amazing TL that inspired me to approach it. So your opinion would be especially appreciated (although of course I would be happy to hear feedback from everyone).
items.original_question: What if Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s UPD: I have updated both the PoD and who is the most likely bride for Pedro. See up-to-date details here and further ( link ). However all the potential consequences of Pedro surviving described in the second part of this message are still very much valid. UPD 2: Please find the TL draft for 1362-1364 in this message ( link ) I've always had a soft spot for Pedro the Cruel (aka Pedro the Just) of Castile. His victory over Henry of Trastamara would have monumental consequences both for Iberian Kingdoms and for Europe in general (I will list some of them further down). While there are a few threads on the forum discussing the possibility of his victory over Henry they are all rather short and usually either discuss earlier PoDs (e. g. Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: The new dynasty came to power having given lavish grants and titles to supporting nobles, and territorial concessions to their royal allies in France and the Crown of Aragon. Henry II’s initial hold on the crown was a tentative one. New men came to the fore demanding a share of the victory, and the king also granted them substantial privileges and lands. Historians have long argued that the first decades of Trastámara rule witnessed the disappearance of the old nobility, a nobility dating to the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, and its replacement by a new nobility. In reality, the transformation was signaled by the rise to prominence of lesser branches of the great old noble houses, with a few new lesser nobles rising to very high status. This promotion in rank was tied to the granting of large estates and to extensive royal privileges. Such erosion of the royal domain and authority had, in turn, disastrous consequences for Castile over the next hundred years. Not unlike France or England in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the rise of the nobility led to waves of violence and instability. Securely grounded in their new economic power and high standing, the Castilian nobility challenged royal authority and even coveted, as was the case in the reigns of John II and Henry IV, the control of the Crown. Pedro unlike Henry is a legitimate king and thus doesn’t need such drastic measures to obtain necessary support. b. In the first half of XIV century one of the main pillars of royal power was municipal nobility (or more precisely non-noble municipal knights). At first kings bought their support against magnates by granting municipal knights’ extensive privileges, but since the latter felt constant pressure by disenfranchised bourgeoisie, they continuously welcomed royal entrenchment in cities and thus by 1340s urban centers were under firm royal control. Once again, quote from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: In less than 50 years the non-noble knights monopolized municipal offices in most Castilian cities, bought most of the land around the cities, and gained control, as they did in Burgos and Avila, of the most important ecclesiastical benefices. In return the king hoped for, and often received, their military support against the magnates and access to the cities’ fiscal resources. Moreover, as the non-noble knights gained control of their respective cities, they came into conflict with those below them. Pressured from below by the disfranchised petite bourgeoisie, the non-noble knights welcomed royal interference in the affairs of the cities and, by the 1340s, the takeover of municipal administration by royal officials (the regimiento) became a political reality. For a brief period, royal control of the urban centers became one of the most significant gains of the Castilian monarchy, but then the disorders of the late fourteenth century weakened royal control anew. IOTL many cities supported Pedro against Henry and thus were severely punished by victorious Trastamaras which greatly weakened both cities themselves and royal control over them. Thus, if Pedro retains his throne Castile is a lot more centralized with a strong royal power based on resources from a reasonably large royal domain as well as prosperous cities under firm royal control which is a stark contrast to magnate-dominated early Trastamara Spain. 2. Pedro IOTL had a firm alliance with Portugal. His uncle Pedro of Portugal helped him in his wars against both Peter of Aragon and Henry of Trastamara. When Pedro of Castile was slain, it was Portugal that was the main base for anti-Trastamara action in Iberia. Ferdinand of Portugal, Pedro of Castile’s cousin waged several wars against Trastamaras (first claiming the crown of Castile in his own right, later supporting John of Gaunt’s claim). Pedro of course is a very strong clamant to Portuguese throne in his own right, but he can further cement his claim by marrying Beatrice of Portugal to his son (who presumably should be born in early to mid 1370s roughly similarly to OTL Roger Mortimer birth date and thus ideally match Beatrice). Moreover, before Trastamara coup Portugal and Castile had the same allies and aligned economic interests (both benefited greatly from maritime trade between Northern Europe and Mediterranean, both had Genoa as a most important trade partner and England as a main ally outside of Iberia). IOTL when Portuguese interregnum happened the nobility was split with a significant portion of it supporting Trastamara claim. It were municipal elites of 4 main Portuguese cities (Lisbon, Porto, Coimba and Evora) that bankrolled anti-Trastamara faction. The main reason for these was economic (i. e. retention of profitable maritime trade with Genoa, England etc.) as well as desire to cancel Ferdinand’s pro-noble reforms (which were conducted in order to fund extremely expensive campaigns against Castille). If IOTL Pedro continues to rule Castille, Portuguese municipal elites have no reason to dislike the union with neighboring kingdom (because Ferdinan’s reforms would be unnecessary and Castile and Portugal economic and political interest would continue to be closely aligned) and thus we can encounter Castilian-Portugese union in 1380s. 3. Pedro had an advantage in the War of Two Peters against Peter of Aragon. Presumably if Henry of Trastamara is no longer a threat, he can continue pressing Aragon for economic, political (most important one being the termination of Trastamara support) and perhaps even territorial concessions (getting back Alicante, Elche and Orihuela as part of kingdom of Murcia) 4. If Pedro marries Philippa, presumably John Gaunt and Edmund Langley would have alternative brides. IOTL the marriages happened to establish a claim over kingdom of Castile. ITTL Pedro would have legitimate heirs related to English royal family without such a match and thus daughters of Peter with at best debatable legitimacy are not ideal brides for English prices. Does anybody have suggestions who John and Edmund would marry in such a scenario? 5. Perhaps the most consequential consequence of the PoD is alternative Caroline Phase of HYW. The battle of La Rochelle that crippled English fleet IOTL was won by Castilian navy. If Castile continues to be an English ally, Castilian navy either doesn’t participate or participates on English side. Thus, English are able to get significant reinforcements to Poitou and Saintonge as well as £12,000 that were supposed to be used to pay for service of local troops (IOTL this booty fell to the hands of Castilians). This potentially a least allows English to retain control over Poitou, Saintonge and Angoumois and perhaps even reverse some French gains made in previous years. Moreover with English fleet still dominating the waters around France, the main reason for the disastrous Great Chevauchee of 1373 is gone. ITTL, it makes a lot more sense to bring reinforcements by see, as was done in previous years. Thus, the Caroline Phase of HYW can be radically altered in 1372-1373, perhaps to the extent of it being a draw rather than decisive French victory. All these consequences seem rather juicy, but I am not sure if the marriage of Pedro and Philippa is all that plausible. What do you guys think? (of course if you have comments on consequences of PoD rather than the PoD itself, I would be happy to hear those too).
items.model_answer:
If Peter of Castile married an English princess in the 1360s, the most likely result would be a much deeper Anglo-Castilian alliance, but not automatically the survival of Peter’s regime. The marriage would make Castile a major stake in the Hundred Years’ War and would probably pull England into Iberian politics earlier and more heavily than it did historically.

The first difficulty is legitimacy. Peter was already entangled in scandal: he had married Blanche of Bourbon, abandoned her, favored María de Padilla, and alienated much of the Castilian nobility and church. For an English royal marriage to work, England would need a recognized annulment or some other settlement acceptable to the papacy and major courts. Without that, the marriage would look illegitimate and would worsen Peter’s reputation. But if the marriage were formally accepted, it would give Peter a powerful dynastic partner and a stronger claim to international respectability.

Politically, the marriage would push Castile firmly toward England and away from France. Historically, Peter’s half-brother Henry of Trastámara received French support, including Bertrand du Guesclin and mercenary forces, while Peter eventually turned to the Black Prince for help. An English princess as queen would make that alignment clearer and earlier. France would see Peter’s Castile as an English client or ally, and Henry’s rebellion would become even more useful to French strategy. So the civil war would probably intensify rather than disappear.

England would have stronger reasons to defend Peter. Edward III and the Black Prince would not merely be aiding a temporary ally; they would be defending a royal in-law and perhaps the future inheritance of an English-Castilian child. That could mean earlier English military intervention, more money and troops committed to Peter, and a greater effort to keep control after victories like Nájera in 1367. If Peter and his English wife produced a legitimate son, the stakes would be even higher: England would have a direct dynastic interest in preserving the Petrine line.

But Peter’s main weakness was internal. He had made too many enemies among the Castilian nobility, and his reputation for cruelty and arbitrary rule gave Henry a strong domestic base. An English marriage would not solve that. It might even make it worse, because nobles hostile to Peter could portray him as dependent on foreigners and willing to subordinate Castile to English interests. French-backed propaganda would have been very effective on that point.

The biggest strategic consequence would be naval and diplomatic. Castile was a major Atlantic naval power. Historically, after Henry II won, Castile became a valuable French ally, and Castilian ships helped threaten English trade and the Channel. If Peter survived with English support, England might gain access to Castilian naval strength instead. That would improve England’s position in the Bay of Biscay, protect Gascony, and weaken France’s ability to pressure English shipping. A stable Anglo-Castilian alliance could have made the later phases of the Hundred Years’ War more difficult for France.

If Peter still lost and was killed, as he was historically in 1369, the consequences would also be serious. England would have an even stronger grievance against Henry of Trastámara. Instead of John of Gaunt later claiming Castile through marriage to Peter’s daughter Constance, the English crown might claim rights through the English princess or her children, if any existed. That could produce a more direct Anglo-Trastámara conflict and perhaps repeated English expeditions into Iberia. The result might be a longer and more internationalized Castilian succession struggle.

So the most plausible outcome is not a peaceful Anglo-Castilian union, but a sharper division of Iberia into Hundred Years’ War camps: Peter, England, and perhaps Portugal on one side; Henry, France, and likely Aragon on the other. If Peter managed to survive and produce a legitimate heir, Castile could become England’s greatest continental ally and France would lose a crucial partner. But if Peter’s domestic position remained as unstable as it was historically, the marriage would mainly make his fall more consequential, turning the Castilian civil war into an even larger dynastic and international conflict.

items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).

items.question: What If an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia
human_answers: I would highly recommend you watch NojRant's NOT the Origins of Russian Authoritarianism . If you'd like a forum post, read my posts in another thread from here onward to here : they briefly go over parts of what you're interested in, and some of it is repeated below. If you want good detail, I'd recommend Robert K. Massie's book Peter the Great . tl;dr - clothes were only a small part of the reforms, there was major modernization of the economy, education and the legal system, and you seem to have a very, very stereotyped and caricaturish understanding of the topic to speak with such confidence. The problem with the reforms was not in their superficiality, but that most of them required follow-through by Peter's successors that, for reasons I'll get into, did not happen until Catherine II some 40 years later. A highly ideological statement if ever I've heard one. Define what it means to be 'European' in clear terms. Absolutism is actually a major benefit in this situation, mainly because it is not a parliament. Parliament is essentially a tool for the ruling class to give themselves endless privileges and benefits: a ruling class composed of rural nobility would see urbanization as a threat to their power over their tenants (and ultimately their wealth) and pursue policies that deurbanize the country, whereas one dominated by bourgeois interests would be enriched by urbanization. Urbanization ultimately leads to a richer, stronger, more industrialized nation overall, while deurbanization does not. As long as Russia has a strong nobility and a comparatively weak bourgeoisie, parliament is a nonstarter for your purposes because the default net effect of parliamentary actions will be to increase nobles' control over their tenants, hence limiting urbanization, hence limiting development of private capital for industrialization. A country with no strong king to keep the nobility in check will increasingly resemble basketcases like high medieval Hungary or early modern Poland, where the nobility could ignore the king as they pleased and even fight each other as warlords ( picrel ). Even in a lesser form, this can have severe consequences: for example, under the Dual Monarchy, the Hungarian half of the empire was granted wide-ranging autonomy, which the Magyar nobility used to systematically and shortsightedly block the development of industry. The result was that Hungary remained agrarian and economically backward, even failing to compete in agriculture - the thing the Magyar nobles had sought to protect - to the extent that Russian grain imported via the Adriatic was undercutting Hungarian grain on the Austrian market. In a strong monarchy, even if the king still has to appease the nobility somewhat, he has control over the spigot of privileges and benefits and only gives them out when he has to, and expects loyal service in return - and can even retract privileges if his position is strong enough, like Ivan the Terrible did in Russia or Charles XI did in Sweden (ref. the Great Reduction ). This is constitutionally impossible with a strong parliament, though the king can always try his luck with a coup or a civil war. Even strong monarchs who retained parliaments as vestigial organs of the state, like Louis XIV, actively avoided involving them in political decisions because they knew that weak parliaments were made strong by getting involved in decisions that could've been made by the king's bureaucrats instead. However, monarchies can be weakened by unexpected deaths, child kings / regencies, changes in dynasty, coups, successful riots by the urban population against taxes, and successful rebellions by uppity nobles. These events force the king to repeal unpopular laws and grant new privileges to the nobles in exchange for their support, because his normal ability to make himself obeyed by his subjects is drastically reduced and he needs to sweeten the pot for them to obey him again. This must be avoided to preserve the king's power and prevent the nobility from pressuring him to grant more privileges. 17th century Russian tsars were weakened by the Time of Troubles, which allowed the nobility to demand a host of new concessions in exchange for their support of Mikhail Romanov as the next tsar. The most notable concession was that their pomestie fiefdoms, which were previously non-hereditary and granted to them in exchange for service to the state, were made hereditary. Russian tsars spent the next century trying to repeal these various privileges with limited success, and were occasionally hampered by new setbacks, such as the 1648 salt riot , which led to tighter restrictions on serfs being introduced to satisfy the nobility. 18th century Russian tsars were weakened by chronic succession problems, which resulted in the new tsar/tsarina having to bribe the nobility as a class with extra privileges to get them to accept their rule. The reason was that Peter had revised the succession law from male primogeniture to "Whoever the tsar chooses," meaning that the tsar's will could be forged or denied by any member of the imperial family who could bribe the palace guards to support them in a coup. Catherine I, Elizabeth, Catherine II and Alexander I all rose to the throne this way. Doable - NojRants covers this succinctly in the Serfdom section of his video. If you can't avoid the Time of Troubles, then you need to avoid all further destabilizing events which allowed the nobility to wring additional concessions out of the tsar. If you want participation in European scientific exchange, look to the Russian Academy of Sciences. Its alumni included such giants as Lomonosov: they corresponded regularly with their peers in the rest of Europe, and many foreign luminaries visited to teach at the academy, such as Euler. Many advances in cartography, botany and geology came from the work of scientists who had been educated in the Academy or invited from abroad to work there. But given the list of names you chose, I suppose your chief interest in the Enlightenment is politics. Of which I frankly don't see the point. If you want to be welcomed at the salons of Paris and London, dressing in European fashion is a bonus, otherwise you might taken as a neat little foreign curiosity. What led you to this conclusion?

I would like to see that properly thought out! ... but: You'd probably need to address the "modernisation challenge" that any Eastern European polity would face and that stems from the divergent socio-economic foundations on which society rested in Western and Eastern Europe respectively. This hearkens back to the Middle Ages and the long-term demographic consequences of the Mongol devastations and the division of labour that only became more and more entrenched over the centuries: The High Middle Ages saw a trend towards slow re-urbanisation, communalism, development of crafts, revitalisation of trade, a new surge in scholarship and education, and while the epicentres of this were in Italy, France, along the Rhine and across the channel in England, this was, in the 11th and 12th centuries, a trend that spread everywhere, towards the North and towards the East. And so, even before the conquest of the Americas by Western European powers, Eastern Europe became tendentially focused on exporting unprocessed raw materials while Western Europe developed proto-capitalist structures and more and more complex structures of value addition - and while the latter fomented the growth of a bourgeoisie, the latter could do with mostly just landowners and peasants. items.model_answer:
If Russia had modernized earlier and more thoroughly, the biggest likely change is that the Russian Empire would have entered the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with stronger state capacity, a broader educated middle class, a larger industrial economy, and less explosive social tension. That could have made the collapse of 1917 less likely, though not impossible.

The key issue is what “modernization” includes. If it only meant more factories, railways, weapons, and bureaucracy while preserving autocracy and landlord power, Russia might simply have become a more efficient authoritarian empire. It could have performed better militarily and economically, but the underlying conflicts among peasants, workers, national minorities, liberals, and the monarchy would still have remained. In that case, modernization might even have intensified unrest by creating a larger urban working class and more politically conscious society without giving them channels for representation.

But if modernization had been deeper—earlier abolition of serfdom, land reform, mass education, legal equality, professional administration, industrial investment, and some form of constitutional politics—Russia’s path could have changed substantially. Abolishing serfdom decades before 1861, or carrying out a more generous land settlement, would have reduced peasant resentment and increased agricultural productivity. Better education and infrastructure would have accelerated economic growth. A more predictable legal system and representative institutions could have given liberals, professionals, workers, and regional elites a stake in the regime rather than pushing them toward revolutionary opposition.

In foreign affairs, a more modern Russia would probably have been a stronger great power. It might have performed better in the Crimean War, avoided or won the Russo-Japanese War, and entered World War I with better railways, logistics, industry, and military organization. If so, the catastrophic wartime breakdown that helped cause the February Revolution might not have occurred. A stronger Russia could also have changed the balance of power in Europe: Germany and Austria-Hungary would have faced a more formidable eastern rival, possibly making European diplomacy more cautious—or, conversely, making Germany feel even more encircled and encouraging earlier confrontation.

The most dramatic possible consequence is that there might have been no Bolshevik Revolution, or at least no successful Bolshevik seizure of power. Without the combination of autocratic rigidity, peasant land hunger, urban hardship, military defeat, and state collapse, Lenin’s party would have had far less opportunity. Russia might instead have evolved into a constitutional monarchy or conservative parliamentary state, somewhat like Germany or Japan, though probably still highly centralized and imperial. That would have profoundly altered the twentieth century: no Soviet Union in its historical form, no Stalinist industrialization, no collectivization, and likely a very different global communist movement.

However, modernization would not automatically have made Russia liberal or peaceful. Russia’s size, ethnic diversity, weak civic institutions, and tradition of centralized rule would still have posed serious problems. A modernized Russia might have become a powerful nationalist empire, suppressing Poles, Ukrainians, Finns, Caucasian peoples, and Central Asians more effectively. It might also have pursued expansion more aggressively in Asia and Eastern Europe. Economic modernization can strengthen democracy, but it can also strengthen authoritarian states.

So the most plausible answer is: earlier, more thorough modernization would probably have made Russia richer, militarily stronger, and more administratively stable, while reducing the chances of the 1917 revolutionary collapse. It might have produced a constitutional imperial Russia rather than a Soviet one. But if modernization had not included political reform and social compromise, it could have merely postponed crisis or produced a stronger authoritarian empire rather than a freer society.
